title: Webb Finds Star Duo Forms ‘Fingerprint’ in Space
caption: Dust rings around the binary star Wolf-Rayet 140, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope

recognition.text: Published in the ESA/Webb image archive. No published rating.

story: At least 17 pink-orange rings spread out like ripples from a pair of bright stars at the centre of this Webb image, set against black space scattered with tiny red galaxies. The pair is known as Wolf-Rayet 140.

Each ring formed when the two stars swung close and their stellar winds collided, compressing gas into dust. Their orbit brings them together about once every eight years, so, like tree rings, the dust loops keep time. The orbit is elongated; only when the stars come about as close as Earth is to the Sun is the gas squeezed enough to make dust.

One star is a Wolf-Rayet star, born with at least 25 times the Sun's mass and nearing its end. Its powerful winds carry carbon from deep inside, which cools and is kneaded into dust where the winds meet. This study gives the best evidence yet that such stars make carbon-rich dust that survives between the stars.
scale: The pair lies just over 5000 light-years from Earth, according to the release.

understand.summary: Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI) imaged the rings at 7.7 microns (shown in blue), 15 microns (green) and 21 microns (red).
understand.eye: Webb detects infrared light, which the human eye cannot see, so the colours are a translation of mid-infrared wavelengths.

explore: Webb's MIRI instrument sees the longest infrared wavelengths, ideal for cool dust. Astronomers expect a few thousand Wolf-Rayet stars in our galaxy, but only about 600 have been found. Swept-up material around them may help form new stars, and there is some evidence the Sun formed that way.
alt: A pair of bright stars at the centre with at least 17 pink-orange concentric dust rings, on a black background with tiny red galaxies.
